bib.title: Beyond RAG for Agent Memory: Retrieval by Decoupling and Aggregation

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Beyond RAG for Agent Memory: Retrieval by Decoupling and Aggregation" (xMemory), Zhanghao Hu, Qinglin Zhu, Runcong Zhao, Di Liang, Hanqi Yan, Yulan He, Lin Gui (King's College London; Tencent Yuanbao). arXiv:2602.02007v4 [cs.cl], 12 May 2026, marked "Preprint".

COVERAGE: Pages 1-26 of 26 (all of it), 91,844 chars, extracted with pypdf. Body is pp.1-10, references pp.10-12, appendix pp.13-26 (setup, tables 4-10, Fano derivation, case study, limitations, prompts). Nothing skipped. Figure images were not viewed; only the text extraction and captions were read.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. xMemory has the best average on LoCoMo for all three readers and uses fewer tokens than Nemori, A-Mem and MemoryOS.
 number: Qwen3-8B 34.48/43.98 BLEU/F1 at 4711 tok/query; Llama-3.1-8B 24.73/34.77 at 5540; GPT-5 nano 38.71/50.00 at 6581
 setup: LoCoMo, 4 answerable categories (adversarial omitted); baselines Full Memory, Naive RAG (top-20 chunks), LightMem, Nemori, A-Mem, MemoryOS; text-embedding-3-small; greedy decoding, temp 0; same backbone for construction and answering. Table 1 values: Nemori Qwen 31.44/40.88 at 7755 tok; Naive RAG Qwen 27.95/36.48 at 8633; Full Memory Qwen 25.83/33.54 at 18536; Nemori GPT-5 nano 36.65/48.17 at 9155; Nemori Llama 22.21/32.95 at 9803.
 quote: "with Qwen3-8B, average BLEU/F1 improves from 31.44/40.88 for Nemori to34.48/43.98; with GPT-5 nano, it improves from 36.65/48.17 to38.71/50.00while reducing token usage from 9155 to6581per query."
 where: p.6, Table 1

2. Gains are largest on multi-hop and temporal questions (Qwen3-8B, Table 1).
 number: multi-hop 27.24... see Table 1: xMemory multi-hop 27.24? No. In Table 1 xMemory Qwen is multi-hop 27.24/38.57, temporal 29.58/37.46 (Nemori 25.78/33.76 temporal; Naive RAG 17.21/21.32 temporal).
 setup: LoCoMo, Qwen3-8B
 quote: "xMemory achieves the best average performance, with especially clear gains on multi-hop and temporal questions."
 where: p.6

3. PerLTQA results.
 number: Qwen3-8B 36.24/47.08/42.50 BLEU/F1/R-L at 5087 tok; Llama-3.1-8B 42.68/52.37/47.84 at 6066; GPT-5 nano 36.79/46.23/41.25 at 7307. Baselines on Qwen: Nemori 32.55/42.80/38.05 at 9092; Naive RAG 32.08/41.37/35.95 at 6274; Full Memory 32.73/42.15/36.65 at 25045.
 setup: PerLTQA (~25K tokens avg context, sentence-style answers), same baselines. Caveat: on Llama, LightMem uses 5452 tok and A-Mem 7707 tok, which are fewer than xMemory's 6066. On GPT-5 nano, Naive RAG uses 10756 vs 7307 for xMemory, but LightMem uses 7579 tok, which is slightly more.
 quote: "With Qwen3-8B, it achieves the best BLEU/F1/ROUGE-L at36.24/47.08/42.50while using the fewest tokens; with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, it reaches42.68/52.37/47.84."
 where: p.7, Table 2

4. Ablation (LoCoMo, Qwen3-8B, Table 5, p.18): memory structure alone beats Naive RAG; the full system is best on both quality and tokens.
 number: Naive RAG 27.95/36.48 at 8633 tok; Memory-only 31.81/40.77 at 7236; +Stage I 32.55/40.64 at 6321; +Stage II 33.23/42.55 at 6557; Full 34.48/43.98 at 4711
 quote: "Memory-only improves average BLEU/F1 from 27.95/36.48 for Naive RAG to 31.81/40.77, showing that retrieval over decoupled memory units is more effective than retrieval over flat raw chunks, even with basic similarity matching."
 where: p.7 and p.18. Note Stage I alone lowers F1 slightly (40.64 vs 40.77) while cutting tokens.

5. Revisable structure (split/merge) matters.
 number: freezing both gives 0.00% reassignment, avg 31.30/38.59; w/o split 17.33%, 32.54... precisely: w/o split 31.73/39.18; w/o merge 32.54/40.33 at 26.23%; full 34.48/43.98 at 44.91%. Groups: 1114 w/o both, 651 w/o split, 1122 w/o merge, 642 full; components about 2880 in all settings.
 setup: LoCoMo, Qwen3-8B; "dynamic reassignment ratio" is the fraction of existing components whose group changes during later insertions.
 quote: "Disabling both split and merge freezes the structure, yields 0% reassignment, and reduces average F1 to 38.59, whereas the full system reaches the highest reassignment ratio (44.91%) and the best average F1 (43.98)."
 where: p.8, Tables 8-9 pp.20-21

6. Group size cap of 12 is best; Fano bound is the motivation.
 number: caps 14/12/10/8 give avg F1 42.10/43.98/42.80/41.21; avg components per group 7.47/4.48/3.64/2.58; groups 383/642/805/1111
 setup: LoCoMo, Qwen3-8B. The derivation assumes B=2 bits and 0.85 routing accuracy: n_k <= 2^((B+1)/α) = 2^3.529 ≈ 11.5, rounded to 12. This is a heuristic and the assumed B=2 is not measured.
 quote: "we therefore adopt B= 2 bits, an upper-bounding assumption" ... "nk ≤2 (B+1)/α = 2 3.529 ≈11.5, which we round ton maxk = 12 as the split threshold"
 where: p.8, p.19 (Table 6)

7. Denser evidence and cheaper coverage than RAG, and pruning hurts.
 number: blocks needed to cover all answer evidence: xMemory 5.66 (974.56 tok) vs Naive RAG 10.81 (1979.26 tok) vs RAG+LLMLingua-2 pruning 13.31 (1587.99 tok); pruning F1 34.58 vs 36.48. Multi-hop: xMemory 2-hit 13.14% and multi-hit 12.19% vs Naive RAG 7.82% and 6.53%.
 setup: LoCoMo, Qwen3-8B; "evidence units" are the content words of the reference answer after stopword removal, a lexical proxy. A block is 1-hit, 2-hit or multi-hit (>=3) by distinct evidence units it contains.
 quote: "pruning reduces token cost relative to Naive RAG, but requires more blocks and yields lower accuracy, consistent with fragmented evidence after compression."
 where: p.9, Table 3, Table 7 p.20

8. End-to-end cost, including construction (Table 10, p.21): xMemory construction is 421.91k tokens, versus 381.29k for Nemori, 1008.55k for A-Mem, 481.89k for MemoryOS, 125.95k for LightMem, and 0 for Naive RAG and Full Memory. The paper says xMemory has lower total cost than Nemori, MemoryOS and A-Mem. xMemory's construction cost is higher than Nemori's, so the saving comes from inference.
 quote: "xMemory attains the highest average BLEU while using a lower total token cost than Nemori, MemoryOS, and A-Mem."
 where: p.9, Fig 6, Table 10

9. Hyperparameters were fixed across datasets and models, and results are fairly stable near the defaults (Table 4, p.17). Defaults: group cap 12, attach threshold 0.6, post-split clustering 0.65, merge 0.65, kNN neighbourhood 10, Stage I candidate pool 20. Avg F1 at attach 0.5/0.6/0.7/0.8 is 42.51/43.98/42.85/42.28; merge 0.6/0.65/0.7/0.75 is 42.51/43.98/42.14/41.55. Note the thresholds were tuned on the test benchmark (LoCoMo, Qwen3-8B), as far as the text shows.
 quote: "All xMemory hyperparameters are fixed across datasets and backbone models"
 where: p.6, p.16-17

METHOD (for the note)
- Four levels: original messages -> segments (coherent local events, detected incrementally by an LLM boundary detector) -> memory components (LLM-extracted atomic facts, constraints, preferences or state updates, each with text, embedding and a pointer to its source segment) -> groups (aggregated components). pp.3-4, 14.
- Grouping objective: f(P)=SparsityScore+SemScore. SparsityScore = N²/(K Σ n_k²), which favours balanced groups. SemScore is intra-group cosine to the centroid, weighted by a bell-shaped g(s_k) that penalises near-duplicate or isolated centroids. p.4.
- Maintenance: attach a new component to the nearest group if cosine > τ (0.6), else create a new group. Split a group when its size exceeds the cap, via graph-based local clustering with a size-based fallback. Merge a group that has only one component into its nearest neighbours. The operation chosen is the one that most improves f(P). Attach is online; split and merge run periodically or when thresholds are crossed. pp.14-15.
- Retrieval Stage I: greedy selection of a "backbone" over groups, then components, trading off kNN coverage gain against query similarity (Eq. 4). Stage II: add segments, then messages, only if the marginal reduction in reader uncertainty is positive; uncertainty is predictive entropy of the next-token answer distribution. Stop when no candidate reduces it. For GPT-5 nano, which exposes no logits, GPT-4.1-mini serves as the entropy proxy. pp.5, 15-16.
- Alternative framing: "decoupling before aggregation", versus summary-centric hierarchies that compress progressively and blur distinguishing details.

LIMITS
- Authors concede (p.22): only LoCoMo and PerLTQA; extra construction cost, so with "very few queries after memory construction, simpler retrieval methods may be preferable"; relies on LLM-generated components and summaries, so extraction errors may hurt retrieval; privacy, stale or wrong memory risks.
- Not shown (my reading): no significance tests, seeds or variance reported. Metrics are BLEU/F1/ROUGE-L only, with no LLM judge. Only small readers (8B, nano). The same backbone builds memory, so there is no cross-model construction test. No latency or wall-clock numbers. Token counts include "auxiliary calls", but construction tokens are reported only for Qwen3-8B on LoCoMo. The GPT-5 nano uncertainty uses a different proxy model (GPT-4.1-mini), which adds an inconsistency. The adversarial LoCoMo category is omitted. Baseline settings (top-20 for Naive RAG) are those the authors chose. Baseline numbers appear to be the authors' reruns, not published figures. Fano constants are assumed, not measured. Context lengths are small (about 18K and 25K tokens), so scaling to long-lived memory is untested.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
MemGPT (Packer et al. 2023); Generative Agents (Park et al. 2023); MemoryBank (Zhong et al. 2024); LightMem (Fang et al., ICLR 2026) as the baseline and for the cost-reporting setup; Nemori (Nan et al. 2025); A-Mem (Xu et al., NeurIPS 2025); MemoryOS (Kang et al., EMNLP 2025); Zep (Rasmussen et al. 2025); CAM (Li et al.); LeanRAG (Zhang et al. 2025), whose "semantic island" idea and hierarchical retrieval it follows; RAPTOR (Sarthi et al. 2024); LLMLingua-2 (Pan et al. 2024); LoCoMo (Maharana et al. 2024); PerLTQA (Du et al. 2024); Lewis et al. 2020 (RAG); Fano's inequality for the group-size bound; the survey "Memory in the age of AI agents" (Hu et al. 2025).

CODE: No code release or link is given in the text. Algorithm 1 (p.16) gives the pipeline pseudocode. Key lines: "if ∆U(s|C, q)>0 then Add s to C", and the retrieval-time equations, Eq. 4 on p.5 and Eq. 1-3 on p.4. The answer prompt for LoCoMo says "The answer should be less than 5-8 words" (p.25), which matters when reading BLEU/F1.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.2): similarity top-k vs summary hierarchy vs decoupled structure. Fastest explanation of the "decouple then aggregate" idea.
- Fig 2 (p.3): xMemory overview, with structuring on the left and two-stage retrieval on the right. Best candidate for the note's diagram.
- Fig 3 (p.8): ablation (a) by retrieval stage, (b) by group size cap. Backs the numbers in Table 5/6.
- Fig 4 (p.8): retroactive restructuring, reassignment ratio vs F1.
- Fig 5 (p.9): evidence hit distribution (1/2/multi-hit) per category. Shows RAG + pruning fragmenting evidence.
- Fig 6 (p.9): total token cost vs BLEU, including construction.
- Fig 7 (p.22): the DoorDash case study ("When did Gina lose her job at DoorDash?"). RAG answers "early March 2023"; xMemory answers "January, 2023" (gold). Best concrete example for teaching. I did not render the figures; the captions were read only from the extraction.

PROBLEMS: The extraction has minor garbling: math is flattened (Eq. 2-4 and the Fano bound readable but with lost formatting), table cells run together in places (for example LightMem Llama 5452 appears as "38.375452"; xMemory Llama "47.846066" means R-L 47.84 and Tok 6066; "14.97" etc. are fine), and Table 4 row labels fuse with values (for example "0.525.36" means value 0.5 then 25.36). Bold best-result markers are lost, so "best" claims come from the text. No embedded instructions found in the PDF. I made a drafting slip in claim 2: the numbers to use are those in its setup line (xMemory Qwen multi-hop 27.24/38.57, temporal 29.58/37.46; Nemori temporal 25.78/33.76; Naive RAG temporal 17.21/21.32, all from Table 1). I could not verify these against the table as printed beyond the extraction, and the claim 5 "w/o split" reassignment figure is 17.33% (Table 8). The extracted text is at /tmp/xm.txt, a scratch copy.
